messages.content:
Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)


Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
We are given finite nonempty sets \(A_i\) of positive integers such that

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)
\]

for all positive integers \(i,j\). We want to minimize

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250}\max A_d.
\]

The divisors of \(250=2\cdot 5^3\) are

\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250.
\]

We will show the minimum possible value is \(\boxed{499}\).

---

## 1. Structure forced by the intersection condition

Taking \(i=j\), we get

\[
|A_i|=i.
\]

If \(a\mid b\), then

\[
|A_a\cap A_b|=\gcd(a,b)=a=|A_a|,
\]

so

\[
A_a\subseteq A_b.
\]

Therefore, for any \(i,j\),

\[
A_i\cap A_j=A_{\gcd(i,j)}.
\]

For each positive integer \(n\), define

\[
L_n=A_n\setminus \bigcup_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d<n}} A_d.
\]

The sets \(L_n\) are pairwise disjoint, and every element of \(A_n\) belongs to exactly one \(L_d\) with \(d\mid n\). Hence

\[
A_n=\bigsqcup_{d\mid n} L_d.
\]

Taking sizes,

\[
n=|A_n|=\sum_{d\mid n}|L_d|.
\]

By Möbius inversion, or using the standard identity \(\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n\), we obtain

\[
|L_d|=\varphi(d)
\]

for every positive integer \(d\).

Thus the relevant layers for divisors of \(250\) have sizes

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1 & 2 & 5 & 10 & 25 & 50 & 125 & 250\\
\hline
\varphi(d) & 1 & 1 & 4 & 4 & 20 & 20 & 100 & 100
\end{array}
\]

and their total size is

\[
1+1+4+4+20+20+100+100=250.
\]

Only the layers \(L_d\) with \(d\mid 250\) appear in the sets \(A_d\) for \(d\mid 250\).

---

## 2. Reduction to a scheduling problem

We may assume the \(250\) relevant elements are labeled by \(1,2,\dots,250\), because replacing their labels by the smallest possible labels in the same order cannot increase any \(\max A_d\).

For \(d\mid 250\), let

\[
C_d=\max L_d.
\]

Since

\[
A_d=\bigsqcup_{e\mid d}L_e,
\]

we have

\[
\max A_d=\max_{e\mid d} C_e.
\]

Now think of each layer \(L_d\) as a “job” of length \(p_d=\varphi(d)\). The value \(C_d\) is the completion time of that job. A standard compactness/blocking argument shows that we may assume each layer occupies a consecutive block of labels. Moreover, by swapping blocks whenever a divisor is placed above a multiple, we may assume the low-to-high order of the layers is a linear extension of divisibility:

\[
e\mid f \implies L_e \text{ is below } L_f.
\]

In such an order, for every \(d\mid 250\), all proper divisors of \(d\) appear before \(d\), so

\[
\max A_d=C_d.
\]

Therefore the problem becomes:

> Schedule the jobs \(d\mid 250\) with processing times \(p_d=\varphi(d)\), subject to \(e\) before \(f\) whenever \(e\mid f\), to minimize
> \[
> \sum_{d\mid 250} C_d.
> \]

---

## 3. Optimal order of the layers

The processing times are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1 & 2 & 5 & 10 & 25 & 50 & 125 & 250\\
\hline
p_d & 1 & 1 & 4 & 4 & 20 & 20 & 100 & 100
\end{array}
\]

If two adjacent incomparable jobs \(x,y\) appear in the order \(x,y\) but \(p_x>p_y\), swapping them to \(y,x\) decreases the sum of completion times by \(p_x-p_y\). Hence an optimal linear extension has nondecreasing processing times.

Because \(\varphi(d)\) is nondecreasing along divisibility for these divisors, the unique nondecreasing-processing-time linear extension is

\[
1,\ 2,\ 5,\ 10,\ 25,\ 50,\ 125,\ 250.
\]

The corresponding completion times are

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_1&=1,\\
C_2&=1+1=2,\\
C_5&=2+4=6,\\
C_{10}&=6+4=10,\\
C_{25}&=10+20=30,\\
C_{50}&=30+20=50,\\
C_{125}&=50+100=150,\\
C_{250}&=150+100=250.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the minimum possible value of the desired sum is

\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

---

## 4. Construction attaining the bound

Choose disjoint sets as follows:

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_1&=\{1\},\\
L_2&=\{2\},\\
L_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
L_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
L_{25}&=\{11,12,\dots,30\},\\
L_{50}&=\{31,32,\dots,50\},\\
L_{125}&=\{51,52,\dots,150\},\\
L_{250}&=\{151,152,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For all other positive integers \(d\), choose any disjoint sets \(L_d\) of size \(\varphi(d)\) using positive integers larger than \(250\). Then define

\[
A_i=\bigsqcup_{d\mid i}L_d.
\]

Then

\[
|A_i|=\sum_{d\mid i}\varphi(d)=i,
\]

and

\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigsqcup_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)}L_d=A_{\gcd(i,j)},
\]

so

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j).
\]

For the divisors of \(250\), the maxima are exactly

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max A_1&=1,\\
\max A_2&=2,\\
\max A_5&=6,\\
\max A_{10}&=10,\\
\max A_{25}&=30,\\
\max A_{50}&=50,\\
\max A_{125}&=150,\\
\max A_{250}&=250.
\end{aligned}
\]

Their sum is

\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

Therefore the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
